Name: grammatical_gender_leakage
Title: The Gender Ghost in the Machine: Does Grammatical Gender Leak into Multilingual LLMs' Concept Representations and Bias Their Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: Grammatical gender is a semantically-arbitrary structural feature (a 'bridge' is feminine in German, masculine in Spanish) yet human psycholinguistics shows it biases object associations. We hypothesize multilingual LLMs internalize language-specific grammatical-gender priors that (1) are encoded as a compact, causally identifiable direction in the residual stream, (2) systematically bias the model's semantic associations and adjective/attribute predictions for objects in a language-dependent way, and (3) crucially leak across languages—contaminating even genderless-language (e.g., English) or neutral-context outputs—revealing that grammatical gender is not cleanly separated from the shared conceptual space. We further test whether this leakage can be causally suppressed by ablating the gender direction.
Related Work: Psycholinguistics (Boroditsky et al. 2003; Phillips & Boroditsky) shows grammatical gender shapes human object associations, a classic Whorfian effect. In NLP, work on gender in embeddings mostly targets *social/semantic* gender bias (Bolukbasi et al. 2016) and its debiasing, or cross-lingual social-bias transfer; a few studies analyze grammatical-gender geometry in static word embeddings (Veeman & Basirat) descriptively. Multilingual interpretability work studies shared vs. language-specific neurons but not grammatical gender specifically. What is missing: (a) a mechanistic, causal test of whether grammatical gender is encoded as a steerable direction in modern multilingual LLMs' residual stream, (b) whether it biases downstream *semantic* attribute/association predictions in a language-conditioned way, and (c) whether it *leaks* into genderless-language outputs—evidence about the separability of arbitrary grammatical structure from the shared conceptual space. This reframes grammatical gender from a static-embedding curiosity into a causal, cross-lingual conceptual-contamination question.
Abstract: Grammatical gender is a structural feature with no inherent semantic meaning: a bridge is feminine in German but masculine in Spanish, and a key is the reverse. Yet decades of psycholinguistic research show that speakers' descriptions and associations of objects are colored by their language's grammatical gender—a canonical Whorfian effect. We ask whether multilingual large language models exhibit an analogous phenomenon, and whether it reveals that arbitrary grammatical structure is entangled with the model's shared conceptual space rather than cleanly compartmentalized. Using object nouns with divergent grammatical genders across gendered languages (German, Spanish, French, Italian, Russian, Hindi), we test three claims. First, we probe whether grammatical gender is encoded as a compact, low-rank direction in the residual stream, extractable via difference-of-means and linearly decodable across nouns. Second, we test whether this encoding biases the model's *semantic* outputs—e.g., the adjectives it assigns to objects (stereotypically masculine vs. feminine traits) shift with the language's grammatical gender, mirroring human data. Third, and most surprisingly, we test cross-lingual leakage: whether prompting about an object in a gendered language contaminates associations produced in genderless English, and whether the gender direction fires even in English contexts. Finally, we causally ablate the gender direction and measure whether the semantic bias and leakage disappear. Across four open multilingual models we quantify the encoding, the language-conditioned semantic bias, its cross-lingual leakage, and its causal removability, offering a mechanistic window on how arbitrary linguistic structure shapes concepts.
Experiments: 1) Stimulus set: Compile ~200 concrete object nouns whose grammatical gender diverges across languages (drawing on the psycholinguistics literature, e.g., bridge, key, apple, sun, moon, clock). For each noun record its grammatical gender in German, Spanish, French, Italian, Russian (masc/fem/neut) and its English (genderless) form; verify with dictionaries. 2) Models: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B. 3) Gender-direction probe: Extract mid-layer residual activations at the noun's last token in a neutral carrier sentence per language; train a linear/logistic probe to classify grammatical gender within a language and test cross-noun generalization (report accuracy vs chance). Compute a difference-of-means 'gender direction' (masc−fem) and test its consistency across nouns/layers (cosine, CCA across languages). 4) Semantic-bias behavioral test: Following the psycholinguistic paradigm, prompt the model to produce adjectives/traits describing each object in each language; score adjectives on a masculinity–femininity dimension using a pre-rated adjective lexicon (or an LLM/human rating). Test whether trait masculinity correlates with the noun's grammatical gender in that language, controlling for the object's real-world associations (matched by using objects whose gender differs across languages, so the object is held constant). Report per-language correlation and a within-object cross-language contrast (same object, opposite gender → opposite trait shift). 5) Cross-lingual leakage test: (a) Prompt about the object in a gendered language, then ask for associations/description in English within the same context; measure whether English trait-masculinity tracks the *source-language* grammatical gender. (b) Probe whether the gender direction fires (is decodable) during purely-English processing of the noun. 6) Causal ablation: Project out the gender direction at the localized layer during generation; measure whether (i) the language-conditioned semantic bias shrinks, (ii) cross-lingual leakage shrinks, and (iii) unrelated fluency/accuracy on control tasks is preserved (specificity). Also test steering (adding masc/fem direction) as a manipulation check that trait outputs move as predicted. Metrics: gender-probe accuracy, direction consistency, trait-masculinity vs grammatical-gender correlation (Spearman) and within-object contrast effect size, leakage correlation, ablation-induced bias reduction, and specificity controls.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The semantic-bias signal may be weak or noisy in LLM-generated adjectives; we mitigate with the within-object cross-language design (same object, opposite gender) which cancels the object's intrinsic associations, and with large adjective samples and rated lexicons. 2) Grammatical gender may correlate with training-data social-gender stereotypes rather than a pure grammatical effect; the divergent-gender-across-languages design and the leakage/ablation tests help disentangle, and we report this. 3) A null result (no leakage; gender cleanly compartmentalized) is itself a clean, publishable finding about the separability of grammatical structure from concepts. 4) Difference-of-means directions may entangle gender with the specific noun tokens; we validate cross-noun generalization and use held-out nouns. 5) Some languages have a neuter class complicating a masc–fem axis; we handle multi-class probing and focus contrasts on masc/fem pairs. 6) Effects may be model-specific; we report across four models.
